definition: The Thai telling of the Ramayana, compiled at the court of King Rama I around 1798. It is Thailand's national epic, performed as khon dance-drama, and its scenes line the galleries of Wat Phra Kaew in Bangkok.

The Cambodian Ramayana, known in Khmer as Ramakerti, 'the glory of Rama'. It reshapes the Indian epic for Khmer Buddhist court culture, with its own names and episodes, and is performed in classical dance and shadow theatre.
The hero of the Ramayana and the Ramakien, an exiled prince and an avatar of the god Vishnu. In Thai he is Phra Ram, in Khmer Preah Ream, and Thai kings have taken the name Rama.

The wife of Rama, abducted by the demon king Ravana and rescued after a war. In the Ramakien she is Nang Sida, also called Phra Laksami, and her fire ordeal and later exile are told differently across Southeast Asia.

The white monkey warrior of the Ramayana, son of the wind god and devoted servant of Rama. In the Ramakien he is a trickster and lover as well as a hero, famous for leaping to Longka and carrying a mountain.

A serpent being of South and Southeast Asian religions, guardian of rivers, earth and relics. In Theravada Buddhist countries the naga is honoured, not feared, and naga images guard temple stairways and Buddha images, while the naga guards the Mekong itself.
The rice goddess of Java and Bali, also called Nyai Pohaci Sanghyang Asri in Sundanese tradition. Her body becomes the food plants, and farmers honour her at planting, harvest and storage of rice.

A bird-woman of Southeast Asian Buddhist and courtly art, human above the waist with wings, tail and bird's feet. Kinnari appear in Thai, Khmer, Lao and Burmese painting, sculpture and dance, often as musicians.

Javanese shadow puppet theatre, in which a dalang narrates epics such as the Ramayana and Mahabharata to gamelan music. Wayang kulit is the best-known form, and the Ramayana cycle remains central to its repertory.

The 'Teaching of the Elders', the Buddhist tradition dominant in Thailand, Laos, Cambodia, Myanmar and Sri Lanka. Its Pali canon contains the Mucalinda story, and its art and festivals shape the naga and kinnari traditions.
